blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Frontend libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.

As a full stack developer, you don't need to be a designer, but you do need to build screens that work for everybody, and to fix layouts without guessing. HTML comes first, because it gives a page its meaning.

### Why the tag you choose matters

A `<div>` means nothing. A `<button>` comes with keyboard focus, Enter and Space handling, and a role that screen readers announce. If you build a button from a `<div>`, you must rebuild all of that by hand, and you probably won't.

blocks.code:
Home Orders

Your orders

Recent

Order 9001

Delivered on 31 October.

blocks.title: Landmarks help assistive technology, and readers of your code

blocks.text:
| Element | Use |
|---|---|
| `h1` to `h6` | An outline of the page; don't skip levels for size, as CSS handles size |
| `a` | Goes somewhere: it has a URL |
| `button` | Does something on this page |
| `ul`, `ol` | Lists, including navigation |
| `table` | Tabular data, not page layout |
| `label` | Names a form control |
| `img` with `alt` | Describes an image; `alt=""` for decoration |
If it changes the URL, and could be opened in a new tab, use `<a>`. If it performs an action, use `<button>`. An `<a onClick>` with no `href` is a common bug.
blocks.title: Link or button?

blocks.text: ### Forms

blocks.code:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="email">

  <label for="age">Age</label>
  <input id="age" name="age" type="number" min="18" max="120">

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Plan</legend>
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="free" checked> Free</label>
    <label><input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro"> Pro</label>
  </fieldset>

  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
blocks.title: A form that works without any JavaScript

blocks.text:
- A label with `for` makes the label clickable, and gives the input a name for screen readers. A placeholder isn't a label: it vanishes as soon as someone types.
- `type="email"` brings up the right keyboard on phones, and basic validation.
- `autocomplete` helps users and password managers.
- A `<button>` inside a form submits it by default. Use `type="button"` for anything else, because this surprises many developers.
Anybody can bypass it with curl. It exists for quick feedback. Your Spring Boot API must validate everything again.
blocks.title: Client validation isn't security

blocks.text:
### What the browser does with HTML

The browser parses HTML into the **DOM**, a tree of objects, and CSS into the CSSOM. These become a render tree, followed by layout (where everything goes), paint (the pixels) and compositing (combining layers). A `<script>` without `defer` blocks parsing, which is why modern pages use `<script type="module">` or `defer`.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[HTML] --> B[DOM]
  C[CSS] --> D[CSSOM]
  B --> E[Render tree]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Layout]
  F --> G[Paint]
  G --> H[Composite]
blocks.title: From bytes to pixels
Key points
blocks.text:
- Choose elements for meaning
- Buttons act, links navigate
- Every input needs a label
- Validate again on the server

sections.title: The CSS cascade, specificity and the box model

blocks.text:
Most CSS frustration comes from not knowing which rule wins, and how sizes are calculated.

### Which rule wins?

The browser decides in this order: importance, then specificity, then source order.

| Selector | Specificity (ids, classes, elements) |
|---|---|
| `p` | 0, 0, 1 |
| `.note` | 0, 1, 0 |
| `p.note` | 0, 1, 1 |
| `#main` | 1, 0, 0 |
| `#main .note p` | 1, 1, 1 |
| Inline `style=""` | Beats all of these |
| `!important` | Beats normal rules; avoid it |

blocks.title: Which colour is the text?

blocks.text:
Keep specificity low and even, with classes rather than ids. If you find yourself adding `!important`, a specificity battle has begun.

### Inheritance

Some properties, such as `color` and `font-family`, pass down to children. Others, like `margin` and `border`, don't. That's why setting a font on `body` works for the whole page.

### The box model

Every element is a box: content, padding, border and margin.

blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  A[Content] --> B[Padding] --> C[Border] --> D[Margin]
blocks.title: The box, from inside to outside
Width calculation

blocks.text:
Almost every project sets `border-box` globally, because it matches how people think about sizes.

**Margin collapse:** vertical margins between adjacent blocks merge into the larger of the two, rather than adding up. It's a common source of "why is this gap wrong?" Flex and grid children don't collapse, and many teams use `gap` instead.

### Units

| Unit | Relative to | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `px` | Fixed | Borders, small details |
| `rem` | Root font size | Font sizes, spacing; respects user settings |
| `em` | Parent font size | Component-relative spacing |
| `%` | Parent's size | Widths |
| `vw`, `vh` | Viewport | Full-screen sections |
| `dvh` | Dynamic viewport | Full height on mobile, where toolbars move |
| `ch` | Character width | Readable line lengths |

Font sizes in `rem` let users' browser settings scale your page, which helps accessibility.

### Display and position

| `position` | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `static` | Default flow |
| `relative` | Offsets from its normal place; anchors absolute children |
| `absolute` | Removed from flow; placed against the nearest positioned ancestor |
| `fixed` | Placed against the viewport |
| `sticky` | Normal until it reaches a scroll threshold, then sticks |

`z-index` only works within a **stacking context**, which is why `z-index: 9999` can still lose. A parent with a transform or its own z-index creates a new context that contains its children.

**"z-index isn't working."** It needs a positioned element, and it only compares within a stacking context. A parent with `transform`, `opacity` below 1 or its own `z-index` traps its children in that context.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- Importance, specificity, then order
- Keep specificity low
- Use border-box everywhere
- z-index works within a stacking context
### Flexbox: one direction

blocks.title: Common Flexbox patterns

blocks.text:
| Property | Direction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `justify-content` | Main axis | Distribute along the row |
| `align-items` | Cross axis | Align across the row |
| `flex: 1` | Item | Grow to fill the space |
| `gap` | Container | Space between items |

A flex item won't shrink below its content's minimum size by default. A long code line or table inside `.content` then overflows the page. `min-width: 0` on the item fixes it, and it's one of the most useful lines to know.
blocks.title: The min-width trap

blocks.text: ### Grid: two directions

blocks.title: Common Grid patterns

blocks.text:
The second pattern fits as many 260px columns as possible, and stretches them to fill the row. It replaces many media queries.

| Choose | When |
|---|---|
| Flexbox | Items in a line: toolbars, nav bars, small rows |
| Grid | Rows and columns matter: page layouts, galleries |

### Responsive design

Start with the small screen, and add rules as space grows. This needs `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` in the head, without which phones render a shrunk desktop page. Container queries let a component respond to its own container rather than to the screen, which suits reusable components.

### Modern CSS features worth knowing

| Feature | Use |
|---|---|
| CSS variables `--color-accent` | Themes, dark mode |
| `clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem)` | Fluid sizes with limits |
| `:has()` | Style a parent based on its children |
| `aspect-ratio` | Keep video and image shapes, avoid layout shifts |
| Nesting | Group related rules natively |

### Tailwind and CSS approaches

| Approach | Good | Watch out |
|---|---|---|
| Plain CSS or modules | No tooling lock-in; full control | Naming and organisation |
| Tailwind utility classes | Fast, consistent, small CSS output | Long class lists; learning names |
| CSS-in-JS | Dynamic styles | Runtime cost in some libraries |
| Component libraries | Fast start, accessible widgets | Harder to customise |

This site uses Tailwind. Whatever you choose, you still need the CSS underneath to debug: use the browser's Elements panel, where you can see which rules apply and which are crossed out.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Flex for a line, grid for rows and columns
- min-width 0 fixes overflowing flex items
- Design mobile first
- Learn CSS beneath any framework

Accessibility means that people using keyboards, screen readers or magnification can use your product. It's also a legal requirement in many places, and it improves things for everybody. Interviewers increasingly ask about it, and few candidates can answer.

### The rules that catch most problems

| Rule | Check |
|---|---|
| Keyboard works | Unplug the mouse: can you Tab to everything, and use it? |
| Visible focus | Can you see where focus is? Never remove `outline` without a replacement |
| Real elements | `button`, `a`, `label`, and proper headings |
| Text alternatives | `alt` on images, names on icon buttons |
| Contrast | Body text needs at least 4.5:1 under WCAG AA |
| Colour isn't the only signal | Add text or icons to red error states |
| Errors are announced | Link errors to their fields |

### ARIA: only when HTML can't do it

The first rule of ARIA is that if a native element exists, use it. ARIA only changes what's announced, and adds no behaviour.

blocks.text:
### Dialogs

A modal is harder than it looks: focus must move in, Tab must stay inside, Escape must close it, and focus must return to where it came from. The native `<dialog>` element with `showModal()` handles much of this. In React, a tested component library is usually better than writing your own.

### Single-page apps

When a React app changes route, no page load happens, so screen readers hear nothing. Move focus to the new page's heading, and update `document.title`. Announce dynamic changes such as "Saved" through an `aria-live` region.

### Testing

| Tool | Finds |
|---|---|
| Keyboard only | Focus order and traps |
| Lighthouse or axe | Missing names, contrast, roles |
| Screen reader (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on Mac) | What's really announced |
| Testing Library's `getByRole` | Encourages accessible markup in tests |

Automated tools catch only some of the issues, so do a manual keyboard pass as well.

**"How do you make a custom dropdown accessible?"** First ask whether a native `select` will do. If not, use a tested library, since keyboard navigation, focus and ARIA roles are all needed, and it's easy to get wrong.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- Native elements first
- Everything works by keyboard
- ARIA adds meaning, not behaviour
- Test with a keyboard, then tools

The layout: one column on phones, two from 768px

blocks.text:
### What each decision does

| Line | Why it's there |
|---|---|
| `grid-template-areas` | The layout reads like a picture, and is easy to change at a breakpoint |
| `min-width: 0` on `.content` | Lets wide children scroll instead of stretching the grid |
| `auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr)` | Stat cards wrap without a media query |
| `.table-wrap` scrolling | Wide tables are the most common cause of sideways page scroll on phones |
| `100dvh` | Fills the screen even as mobile browser toolbars move |
| `aria-current="page"` | Tells screen readers, and gives you a CSS hook, for the active link |

### Theming with CSS variables

blocks.title: Light and dark from one set of names
Setting the theme before first paint, to avoid a flash

blocks.text:
Put that script inline in `<head>`, since a bundled script runs too late and the page flashes the wrong colours. This site does exactly this.

### Motion, carefully

Animate `transform` and `opacity`, which the browser can usually composite without layout or paint. Animating `width`, `height` or `top` forces layout, and can stutter.

blocks.title: Respect people who get motion sickness
Key points
blocks.text:
- Name grid areas for readable layouts
- Wrap tables so that they scroll alone
- CSS variables make theming simple
- Animate transform and opacity

Most developers use only a fraction of DevTools. A few features save hours.

### Elements panel

| Task | How |
|---|---|
| Why is this colour wrong? | Styles pane: crossed-out rules lost the cascade |
| What size is it, really? | Computed pane shows the box model |
| Why does it overflow? | Add `outline: 1px solid red` to `*` for a moment |
| Test a hover or focus state | Force state with `:hov` |
| Grid and flex layouts | Click the `grid` or `flex` badge for an overlay |
| What's stacked on top? | The Layers panel, or check for a stacking context |

### Console

blocks.code:
console.table(orders);                   // arrays of objects as a table
console.time('filter'); run(); console.timeEnd('filter');
$0;                                      // the element selected in the Elements panel
$$('button').length;                     // all matching elements
copy(orders);                            // copies a value to the clipboard
blocks.title: Useful console tools

blocks.text:
### Sources: real breakpoints

Stop adding `console.log` everywhere. Add `debugger;` or click a line number. Conditional breakpoints stop only when, say, `id === 42`. Logpoints print without changing code. **Pause on exceptions** stops exactly where an error is thrown. Source maps show your original TypeScript.

### Network panel

| Check | Tells you |
|---|---|
| Status and response body | What the server really said |
| Request headers | Was the token or cookie sent? |
| Timing tab | Waiting (server) or downloading (size)? |
| Throttling | How it feels on a slow connection |
| Copy as cURL | Reproduce it in a terminal, or send to a backend developer |
| Preflight OPTIONS | Whether CORS failed there |

A red CORS error usually hides the response from JavaScript, but the Network panel can still show its status. Check the backend logs as well.

### Application panel

Inspect cookies with their flags, localStorage, sessionStorage, service workers and cache. Clearing site data here is the quickest way to rule out stale state.

### React DevTools

The Components tab shows props, state and hooks for any component, and you can edit them live. Its "why did this render?" option in the Profiler explains renders. Search by name to find what's on screen.

### A debugging routine

blocks.title: Debugging a UI bug

blocks.text:
This narrows any bug into one of four layers, in minutes. It's also a good answer to "how do you debug?"

### Errors in production

Minified stack traces are useless without source maps. Upload maps to an error tracker such as Sentry, rather than serving them publicly. Log the release version with every error, so that you know which deployment introduced it.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Read crossed-out rules
- Use breakpoints, not only logs
- Check the Network panel first
- Narrow bugs layer by layer
#### Semantic HTML

items.question: Why is a clickable div worse than a button?
items.answer: It has no keyboard focus, no Enter or Space handling and no role for screen readers. A button provides them all.

items.question: A button in a form reloads the page when clicked. Why?
items.answer: Its default type is submit. Use `type="button"`, or handle the submit event.

items.question: Why isn't a placeholder a substitute for a label?
items.answer: It disappears on input, often has low contrast, and isn't reliably announced.

blocks.text: #### The CSS cascade, specificity and the box model

items.question: A div has width 200px, padding 10px and border 2px with content-box. How wide is it in total?
Two blocks with margins of 30px and 20px sit one above the other. What's the gap?
items.answer: 30px. Vertical margins collapse to the larger value.

items.question: Why use rem for font sizes?
items.answer: It respects the user's browser font setting, whereas px ignores it.

blocks.text: #### Layout with Flexbox and Grid

items.question: A long code block makes a flex layout overflow. What's the fix?
items.answer: Add `min-width: 0` to the flex item, so that it can shrink, and let the code scroll.

items.question: How do you make a responsive card grid without media queries?
Why does a page look tiny on a phone even with media queries?
items.answer: The viewport meta tag is probably missing.

blocks.text: #### Accessibility

items.question: Does adding role="button" to a div make it a working button?
items.answer: No. It's announced as a button, but you must also add focus and keyboard handling. Use a real button.

items.question: How do you name an icon-only button?
items.answer: Use `aria-label`, or visually hidden text, and hide the icon from assistive technology.

items.question: What must a modal do with keyboard focus?
items.answer: Move focus inside, keep Tab within it, close on Escape, and return focus when closed.

blocks.text: #### Worked example: a responsive dashboard page

items.question: A wide table makes the whole page scroll sideways on phones. What's the fix?
items.answer: Wrap it in a container with `overflow-x: auto`, and ensure its grid or flex parent has `min-width: 0`.

items.question: Why set the theme with an inline head script?
items.answer: It runs before first paint, so the page doesn't flash the wrong theme.

items.question: Why animate transform rather than left?
items.answer: Transform can be composited without layout, so it stays smooth.

blocks.text: #### Debugging in the browser

items.question: How do you check that a request really sent the auth token?
items.answer: Open the request in the Network panel, and read its headers.

items.question: The API returns the right data, but the screen is wrong. Where do you look next?
items.answer: React DevTools, to check props and state. If they're right, inspect the DOM, then CSS.

items.question: Why use a conditional breakpoint?
items.answer: To stop only on the case you care about, such as one ID in a long list.
